title: Fermionic quantum cellular automata in 2d are trivial
authors: Jeffrey Kwan, David M. Long, Jeongwan Haah
abstract: Fermionic quantum cellular automata (QCA) are automorphisms of local fermionic operator algebras ($\mathbb Z_2$-graded superalgebras) that have bounded spread: they map local operators to nearby operators. We prove that every 2-dimensional fermionic QCA on a locally finite-dimensional algebra is a composition of local automorphisms and a fermionic shift. This is implied by our result that every locally finite-dimensional fermionic invertible subalgebra in a one-dimensional lattice is Brauer trivial, \textit{i.e.}, it is stably bounded-spread isomorphic to a tensor product fermionic algebra.
summary: This theoretical paper proves that fermionic Quantum Cellular Automata (QCA) in two dimensions are mathematically trivial. The authors achieve this by employing sophisticated algebraic tools related to fermionic superalgebras and an inductive geometric process involving 'hemming' and 'pleating.' The result significantly constrains the possible dynamics that can be modeled by local fermionic interactions in 2D lattices.
main_problem: The paper aims to prove that fermionic Quantum Cellular Automata (QCA) in two dimensions are mathematically trivial.
main_result: Every 2-dimensional fermionic QCA on a locally finite-dimensional algebra is shown to be a composition of local automorphisms and a simple fermionic shift.
method: The proof utilizes advanced algebraic techniques, specifically establishing that certain fermionic invertible subalgebras in 1D lattices are 'Brauer trivial,' which then leads to the classification of the 2D QCA.
model_or_system: The system modeled is the fermionic Quantum Cellular Automaton (QCA), which is defined as a $*$-automorphism of local fermionic operator algebras ($\mathbb{Z}_2$-graded superalgebras) possessing bounded spread.
key_observables: The primary observables are the algebraic structure (e.g., $\mathbb{Z}_2$-grading, spectral nondegeneracy) and the geometric property of 'spread' (locality) of the automorphism.
important_parameters: Dimensionality (focus on 2D), the size of the initial 'hole' ($r_0$), and the spread ($\ell$) of the QCA.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption of spectral nondegeneracy for the underlying fermionic algebras and requires the initial hole radius to be sufficiently large relative to the spread.
figures_summary: Figure 7 illustrates the inductive process of expanding a QCA with a hole using operations like hemming, pleating, and ironing to simplify the structure.
paper_structure: The paper builds mathematically by first developing the algebraic machinery for fermionic algebras (spectral nondegeneracy, fermionic commutators), then applying this to finite-dimensional algebras, and finally using an inductive process involving geometric operations (hemming, pleating, ironing) to prove the triviality of the 2D QCA.
why_interesting: This work provides a deep structural classification of quantum dynamics (automorphisms) on fermionic systems, which is crucial for understanding the limitations and symmetries of quantum computation models based on local interactions.

Figure 3. Ancilla (fermion) removal. Any finite depth circuit of local automor- phisms can be rewritten with 4k layers U1, U2, . . . , U4k, where each Uj is a circuit supported on the union Rj of far separated regions (strips in 2d). Each Rj takes up a fraction at most 1/k of all sites. Any (fermionic) ancilla used by layer ja with ja ∈[1, k] can be borrowed from a nearby ancilla in R2k+1 ∪· · · ∪R3k and immediately returned. Each layer just needs O(1) strips to borrow ancillas from, but we give a big enough pool of ancillas by taking k large. The ancillas used by layers jb ∈[k + 1, 2k] are borrowed from R3k+1 ∪· · · ∪R4k; those used by layers jc ∈[2k + 1, 3k] are from R1 ∪· · · ∪Rk;...

Figure 4. Blending QCA γ from α on the left with a trivial Brauer boundary algebra B into bilayer shift QCA β = β1 ⊗β2 on the right. The construction is transcription of the following line of thought. The green squares are mapped according to ϕ onto the fermionic commutant A of B, where ϕ is provided by the Brauer triviality. Then, ϕ take up a part of the codomain so any other potential image must live elsewhere. In particular, the on-site algebras at x = n, n + 1 must map out of that region, so we send them out to the right. This incurs cascading surplus and deficit of local algebras, leading to a chain of local shifts, resulting in β1 and β2.

Figure 5. The pleating and ironing construction used in 6.10. Any QCA α is equivalent to α ⊗(α−1 ⊗α)⊗n (top panel with n = 2 layers). By removing local automorphisms in the circuit for α ⊗α−1 or α−1 ⊗α, adjacent pairs of layers can be blended to the identity in alternating ways, creating a pleating of α [34]. The red segments indicate positions where the action of the pleated QCA differs from a tensor product of α or α−1. This pleating can then be flattened and compressed (or ironed out), simply by rearranging local algebras in space. The result is a QCA β ◦(α ⊗id), where β is a circuit, such that β ◦(α ⊗id) has a reduced spread along the direction of the pleat.
